To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the classification accuracy of multiclass classifiers is a function of a novel measure of separation between classes, called rROC, which is independent of the total number of classes; and (2) this rROC can be used to predict the accuracy of such multiclass classifiers on arbitrarily large, previously unseen sets of classes.

(1) the classification accuracy can be predicted by the rROC of a classifier; (2) the rROC is invariant to the number of classes, and (3) the rROC can be estimated from a small set of data, and can then be used to predict the accuracy on a larger set of classes.

(1) the rROC of a classifier provides an upper bound for the classification accuracy, (2) the rROC can be used to estimate the accuracy for new classes, and (3) the accuracy can be predicted by a simple neural-network-based algorithm that uses only the rROC and the density of classification scores.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental question of machine learning: how to estimate the accuracy on a large set of classes from the performance of a classifier on a small set.

the following questions: How does the accuracy of a classifier change when the number of classes increases? Can we predict this change based on the classifier's performance over a limited set of classes? How can we use such predictions to select a classifier for a given task?
the question: how to predict a classifier’s accuracy on a set of classes that it has never seen, given only its performance on a sample of those classes?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method, "CleAneX", can predict classification accuracies in multiclass classification problems with high accuracy and robustness, when new classes are introduced.
our method is the best for predicting the accuracy of a classifier on a new set of classes.
the CleaneX method, which is based on the reversed ROC and the density of the classification scores, is a novel method to predict the performance of a classifier in a new set of classes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a theoretical framework to estimate classification accuracies on unseen classes and a novel method to do so.
we provide a new method to estimate the accuracy for multiclass classifiers, which uses both the observed accuracy and density of classification scores.

we provide a theoretical framework that can be applied to predict the performance of classifiers on unseen classes, and that we propose a practical algorithm for this task that achieves state-of-the-art results on several real-world datasets.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a classifier’s performance on a limited number of classes can be used to predict its performance on a larger number of classes, provided that its representation of the initial class sample is not affected by the new classes.
the rROC is a powerful tool for understanding and improving the generalization capabilities of multiclass classifiers.
the accuracy of multiclass classification can be predicted from a small number of observed accuracies, without the need for additional training data.
